claims.text: Controlled heat treatments that increase local chemical order in near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni stabilize a primarily single-phase FCC microstructure.
A stable single-phase FCC microstructure underpins the combined high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni can exhibit competing FCC and BCC phases.
Random atomic distribution contributes to mixed or competing phases in the initial alloy.
Annealing just below the solvus followed by controlled cooling can incrementally increase local chemical order without changing overall composition.
Greater local chemical order produces more uniform atomic bonding.
Greater local chemical order reduces lattice distortion.
The bonding and lattice-distortion changes associated with increased local order favor FCC over competing structures.
At lower temperatures, enhanced local chemical order increases ordering-enthalpy contributions relative to lattice-distortion and configurational-entropy effects.
This shift in energetic balance stabilizes FCC in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
FCC inherently provides better strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic fracture toughness.
The more ordered heat-treated alloy will have a higher FCC volume fraction than the disordered baseline.
The more ordered heat-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline.
The more ordered heat-treated alloy will have better low-temperature toughness than the baseline.
The more ordered heat-treated alloy will retain or improve environmental resistance relative to the baseline.
The more ordered heat-treated alloy will retain or improve radiation tolerance relative to the baseline.
An as-cast or rapidly quenched Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline has lower local chemical order and less stable or more mixed phase partitioning.
The proposed mechanism applies only near equiatomic composition and when heat treatment does not cause macroscopic separation into intermetallic compounds.
Excessive annealing time or temperature can cause secondary-phase formation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
